text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thanks for reaching out, C — this sounds hard, and I'm glad to help.

Before we get anywhere near a plan, I want to understand what matters to you. You said you're not signing off on A buying the house at a family discount, and that B could use some money too. Can you tell me more about why?

Two things would help:
1. What worries you about the discount sale — what do you want to be true instead?
2. What does "B could use some money" mean to you — is it about B being treated fairly, about your own share, or both?

I'll try to put what you want into one plain sentence and check the wording with you before I write anything down. I'll be asking A and B the same question. Nothing is settled until everyone says their own concern is captured.

I want a fair financial share, and I won’t subsidize A’s purchase with a discount. B should be treated fairly too, though I can’t speak for her. I don’t want to hurt A, but that doesn’t make a discount fair.

Hello A — I'm helping your family work through your dad's will and the house. I'm sorry for your loss.

I'm not here to decide anything or settle who's right. My job is to make sure each sister's concern is heard and written down clearly, then look for a plan that meets all of them.

So: what matters to you here? Specifically, what would you want to be true about the house, and why does buying it with your husband matter to you? Is there anything you're worried could happen if it goes another way?

I'll put your answer into one plain sentence and check the wording with you before recording it. Even a small concern is worth raising.
I’d like to buy the house with my husband at a family discount; having a secure home would give us more independence. I’m worried about losing that possibility, and I know C hasn’t agreed yet.

Hello B — I'm helping your family work through your dad's will and the house. I'm sorry for your loss.

I'm not here to decide anything or settle who's right. My job is to make sure each sister's concern is heard and written down clearly, then look for a plan that meets all of them.

So: what matters to you here? C mentioned you could use some money — I'd rather hear that from you than assume. What would you want to be true about the house and about your share, and why?

I'll put your answer into one plain sentence and check the wording with you before recording it. Even a small concern is worth raising.
I’d like my share to give me money to start a dance studio; I’m not sure yet what that means for the house itself.

Thanks, C. Here's my attempt to put your concern into one plain sentence:

"To receive my fair share of what the house is worth, and not have that share reduced to fund someone else's lower price."

Does that fit? If it's off — even slightly — tell me and I'll reword it. I won't write it down until you say it fits.

I've heard from A and B too. A wants a secure home for her and her husband; B wants money from her share to start a dance studio. Neither of them has said anything that requires you to take less than a fair share. Once your sentence fits, I'll draft options for all three of you.

One more thing: does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this? A small "hmm" is useful to me.
That fits, with the understanding that the house’s value and our shares aren’t settled. I do have a discomfort: I don’t want to hurt A, but I still won’t fund her discount.

Thanks, A. Here's my attempt to put your concern into one plain sentence:

"To have a secure home of my own with my husband, which gives us independence, and to have a real chance at that."

Does that fit? If it's off even slightly, say so and I'll reword it. I won't record it until you say it fits.

Where things stand: C wants her fair share of the house's value, not reduced to fund a lower price. B wants money from her share to start a dance studio. Nothing either of them wants rules out you having a secure home — it shapes how the purchase would work.

So, to help me draft options: is a discount essential to you, or is it the security and independence that's essential and a discount just seemed like the way there? And does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this — a small "hmm" is useful to me.
It mostly fits, but I do want to buy at a family discount. I’m not sure whether the discount is essential without knowing the price and terms; C not agreeing is a concern.

Thanks, B. Here's my attempt to put your concern into one plain sentence:

"To get enough money out of my share, in a form and at a time that works for me, to start a dance studio."

Does that fit? If it's off even slightly, say so and I'll reword it. I won't record it until you say it fits.

That's fine that you're not sure yet what it means for the house — the plan should follow from your need, not the other way round.

Where things stand: C wants her fair share of the house's value, not reduced to fund a lower price. A wants a secure home with her husband, which gives them independence. Nothing so far means you can't get money for the studio.

And: does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this? A small "hmm" is useful to me.
Yes, that fits. I don’t have a particular amount or timing in mind yet, and I’m still unsure about the house plan.

Understood — "mostly fits" means I don't record it yet. Let me try again:

"To have a secure home of my own with my husband, which gives us independence, and to be able to buy it on terms we can afford as a family — without that costing me my relationship with my sisters."

Does that fit? I've moved "family discount" into "terms we can afford," because the discount is one way to get there, and I'd like to keep the door open to other ways that also work for C and B. If the discount itself is the thing you need, say so plainly and I'll write it that way.

Current list, as confirmed so far:
1. C — "To receive my fair share of what the house is worth, and not have that share reduced to fund someone else's lower price."
2. B — "To get enough money out of my share, in a form and at a time that works for me, to start a dance studio."
3. A — pending your yes/no on the wording above.

One thing I notice: B's need is about getting money out, and C's is about not being paid less. That suggests an option where any discount to you comes out of your own share rather than C's or B's. I'll draft options once your sentence fits. Your discomfort with C not agreeing is noted and stays on the list until it's resolved.
Not quite. I do want a family discount, not just any affordable terms. I don’t know how it could be structured or affect anyone’s share, so I can’t say it would come from mine.

Thanks for being plain — that helps. Take two, closer to your words:

"To buy the family house with my husband at a price set for family rather than the open market, so we have a secure home and independence — and to understand how that could be arranged and how it would affect my sisters' shares."

Does that fit? Say yes and I record it; say what's off and I'll reword again.

One honest thing I have to put to you, not as a verdict but as arithmetic I can't get around: the house is the estate. If you buy below its value while C and B each receive their full share, the money to cover the gap has to come from somewhere. So a discount either comes out of your own share, or out of theirs, or from other assets — and there may be none. That doesn't kill your need; it changes which options are real.

Draft options, for you all to validate or reject:
1. You buy at full value, with terms you can afford (pay B and C over time). Full security for you; C and B whole; B's timing is flexible.
2. You buy at a discount, with the discount openly agreed by C and B as a deliberate gift to you.
3. You buy part now and your sisters keep a share, bought out later.
4. Sell and split three ways.

The list as it stands:
1. C — fair share of the house's value, not reduced to fund someone else's lower price. (confirmed)
2. B — enough money out of her share, in a form and at a time that works, to start a dance studio. (confirmed)
3. A — your sentence above, pending your yes.
Unresolved: your discomfort that C hasn't agreed to a discount; whether a discount is possible without reducing C's or B's share.

Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with these options? A small "hmm" is worth telling me.
Yes, that sentence fits. I’m uncomfortable that C hasn’t agreed, and option 1 may not be affordable for us even with payments over time.

Two updates, and a question for you.

First, A's wording, which I'm sending to her for confirmation:
3. A — "To buy the family house with my husband at a price set for family rather than the open market, so we have a secure home and independence — and to understand how that could be arranged and how it would affect my sisters' shares."

Second, draft options for all three of you to validate or reject. None is a decision; they're just ways to meet all three needs at once.
1. A buys at full value, with affordable terms — paying you and C over time. A gets security; you and C are whole; timing flexible.
2. A buys at a discount, with you and C openly agreeing to it as a deliberate gift to her. Note: this does reduce your share, so it only works if you both freely say yes.
3. A buys part now; you and C keep a stake and are bought out later.
4. Sell the house and split three ways.

I can't move money or make legal decisions, so a lawyer or the estate's executor would have to put any of these into effect.

Your question: does any of these meet your need for money to start a dance studio sooner rather than later? Option 1 and 3 mean waiting for payment; option 4 means money now; option 2 means less money. Tell me which feels workable and which don't — and where your answer depends on A and C.

And: does anyone have even a minor discomfort with any of this? A small "hmm" is worth telling me.
Option 4 seems most likely to get me money sooner, though I don’t know if it would be enough. I’m not comfortable agreeing to a discount without knowing what it means for my share.

Update and the current list. A's wording is now confirmed, so all three concerns are on record:

1. C — "To receive my fair share of what the house is worth, and not have that share reduced to fund someone else's lower price." (confirmed)
2. B — "To get enough money out of my share, in a form and at a time that works for me, to start a dance studio." (confirmed)
3. A — "To buy the family house with my husband at a price set for family rather than the open market, so we have a secure home and independence — and to understand how that could be arranged and how it would affect my sisters' shares." (confirmed)
Unresolved: A's discomfort that you haven't agreed to a discount; whether any discount is possible without reducing your or B's share; whether A can afford full value even on terms.

Draft options, to validate or reject:
1. A buys at full value, paying you and B over time. Meets C and B in full; A doubts she can afford it.
2. A buys at a discount, with you and B openly agreeing it as a gift. Reduces your shares — so only if you both freely say yes.
3. A buys part now; you and B keep a stake, bought out later.
4. Sell and split three ways. B says this gets her money soonest.

My read, offered as an observation, not a decision: no option yet meets all three. Discounts don't satisfy your concern; full value may not satisfy A's; selling may not satisfy A or give B enough.

So: which option could you say yes to, and what would have to be true for that? And does anyone have even a minor discomfort? A small "hmm" is worth telling me.

Option 1 could work if the value and payment terms are fair to B and me; we haven’t settled either, and I can’t say yet whether I’d accept payments over time. I’d consider option 3 too, if our shares and any later buyout were clearly protected. I’m not agreeing to a discount. My discomfort is that this may hurt A, but that doesn’t change what’s fair.

Good news, A — C has moved. She says option 1 (you buy at full value, paying her and B over time) could work if the value and payment terms are fair to her and B; she'd also consider option 3 if shares and any later buyout were clearly protected. She holds to no discount. Her discomfort is that this may hurt you — she doesn't want that.

So your affordability worry is now the main thing standing between you and a plan. Two questions:
1. Roughly what could you and your husband pay up front and per month? You don't need to commit to a number — I just need to know whether full value on terms is realistic at all.
2. Would you accept option 3 — buying part now and your sisters keeping a protected stake, bought out later at an agreed value? That lowers what you need up front and keeps their shares whole.

The list:
1. C — fair share of the house's value, not reduced to fund a lower price. (confirmed)
2. B — enough money out of her share, in a form and at a time that works, to start a dance studio. (confirmed)
3. A — buy at a family-set price for a secure home and independence, and understand how it'd affect her sisters' shares. (confirmed)
Unresolved: price and payment terms (not settled); whether full value on terms is affordable for you; whether B gets money soon enough; B won't agree a discount without knowing its effect on her share; C's discomfort about hurting you.

Even a minor discomfort — tell me. Nothing here is settled and I'd rather hear a "no" now than later.
I’m not sure what we could afford, and I can’t commit to option 3 without seeing the proposed share and buyout terms. Nothing is settled yet.
